name: Gully Left of Zumie's Thumb aka Smith's Route
text: [overview] Moderate mixed ground and steeper snow make for a leg workout until the final 300 feet, where difficulty rises.
[overview] Ascend Lamb's Slide beyond Zumie's Thumb and enter the gully on the thumb's left, where good timing brings steep neve and easy mixed pitches.
[overview] Where the snow ends, a pillar of rock is flanked by chimneys.
[approach] Skirt Chasm Lake on its north side (in winter the frozen lake can be crossed) to reach Mills Glacier beneath the east face, where Lamb's Slide begins.

name: Lamb's Slide
text: [overview] The obvious chute along the base of the east face's lower section, with the Glacier rib dividing it from the Flying Dutchman.
[overview] expect rockfall, plus snow or ice that is very firm, and wear a helmet.
[approach] Skirt Chasm Lake on its north side (in winter the frozen lake can be crossed) to reach Mills Glacier beneath the east face, where Lamb's Slide begins.
[approach] The slide is the clear couloir cutting across the base of the lower east face, with a rib of the glacier dividing it from the Flying Dutchman.
[approach] It is a snow or ice climb of about 1,000 ft at up to roughly 50 degrees, and is the usual way to reach Broadway.

name: North Chimney
text: [overview] Often written off as a miserable approach to The Diamond over loose rock in summer, or loose snow in winter, yet in spring it becomes a decent mixed route.
[overview] It starts as an obvious snow gully rising to Broadway and grows steadily more difficult, with the steepest drytooling on the final pitch.
[overview] Move left at the end, hack a way across a snow flute, and roll onto Broadway.
[approach] Continue past the lake to Mills Glacier.

[approach] The chimney is right of center on the lower east face, directly below Broadway and the Diamond, and follows the large left-slanting chimney above the highest snow on the face other than Lamb's Slide.
[descent_text] The rappel line from Broadway leads to Mills Glacier and needs two ropes.

name: The Eighth Route

text: [detailed_rack] Pickets if required;

name: Trough, The
text: [overview] The longest of the three or four snowfields on Long's northwest face, visible from Estes and from the trail past Black Lake.
[overview] Firm corn snow is best;
[overview] dangerous, absent, deep or slushy snow is worse.
[overview] Light hiking boots suit the approach, then switch to mountaineering boots and crampons, and leave the pack where the snow ends.
[detailed_rack] Crampons and an ice axe are advised, avalanche gear is wise, and rockfall from above is a risk.
[approach] Park at the Glacier Gorge Junction trailhead and follow signs past the lakes to Black Lake.
[approach] Scramble over talus and ledges to the snow;
[approach] the Trough is the longest finger of snow reaching into the northwest face of the peak, and it is visible from much of the hike after Black Lake.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
[descent_text] The snow meets the Keyhole route at the Narrows, where parties continue to the summit by the Homestretch;
[descent_text] leave the pack at the top of the snow if you are going on.
[descent_text] Descend by ski, glissade or crampons down the Trough, or reverse the Keyhole route through the boulderfield back toward Bear Lake.
[descent_text] Rocks fall from the Keyhole route above, and the snow can be unstable, so wear a helmet and check the forecast.
[descent_text] Carry an axe and crampons.

name: Noxious Fumes
text: [overview] Mostly a steep snow climb, with a pair of mixed pitches;
[approach] Follow the Claim Jumper approach from the McCullough Gulch trailhead to the beaver ponds, then hike west toward the large terminal moraine of the rock glacier.
[approach] In winter the gulch road is closed by snow, which adds distance but little gain.

text: [detailed_rack] To protect this climb, take assorted snow, ice and rock hardware.
[descent] From the notch, either walk the ridge over Powell and Thatchtop, or go northwest down toward Andrews Glacier.

name: Big Mac Couloir
text: [overview] Steep couloir on the left of the large mid-face buttress, mostly snow plus ice with a little rock;

[approach] Start at the Glacier Gorge Trailhead and, after the second bridge, take the winter trail past Mills Lake and Jewel Lake to Black Lake (or reach it by way of Solitude Lake), then climb an easier iced section toward McHenry's Peak.

name: Concrete Shoes Won't Help Ya In Da River
text: [overview] From ledges of broken rock at the right, climb a corner filled with snow and ice.
[overview] When the icefall appears on the left (the ice crux), climb it, pull over a small roof onto a second fall, and continue up the narrow gully to additional ice and a large ledge.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
[descent_text] The road is closed to vehicles in winter, and the walk down it is long, so budget daylight and be ready for snow-covered pavement.

name: West Couloir
text: [overview] The other option is being dropped on the west side, hauling gear across, and descending the Navajo snowfield.
[what_to_bring] ice axes — two were handy from about a third of the way up
[descent_text] The alternative is to carry gear over the notch and descend the Navajo snowfield on the far side, which is a long way round.

name: Tyndall Gully
text: [overview] A prominent couloir between Hallett's summit and the Tyndall Glacier, mostly cut off from the glacier by a rib of rock.
[overview] It is a short snow climb, but the approach runs the whole length of Tyndall Gorge.
[detailed_rack] Pickets, or possibly a modest set of rock gear for the couloir sides, would give protection.
[approach] Snow slopes below the face can slide, so check the avalanche forecast.

name: Ghost Dancer Couloir
text: [approach] Two better options are suggested: continue over Audubon's summit to the Audubon-Paiute col, then drop down steep snow more directly to the foot of the northeast face (crampons and axes needed);
[approach] or drop from the east-ridge saddle on steep snow to Upper Coney Lake and follow the drainage up to the face.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

name: Pervertical Sanctuary
text: [approach] Scramble around the north side of the lake beneath the east face and aim for North Chimney, the hidden gully below the middle of the Diamond with a snow tongue reaching into it;
[approach] North Chimney is loose fourth and low fifth class (about 5.4) with snow early in the season, so keep out from under other parties and expect rockfall.
[descent_text] Four more rappels end on the snowfield;

name: Pigs in Space
text: [overview] To get out, walk or scramble north toward Andrews Glacier and descend it.
[detailed_rack] Carry crampons and tools for snow, and one set of rock protection for the 5.8 approach climbing.

name: North Couloir
text: [overview] Snow route in the main couloir that divides the north side of Potosi Peak.
[overview] The top is usually free of cornices, though steeper to the climber's right.
[overview] Turn right and cross the snowfield on the way to the top, or head south down the gully until the western ledges can be scrambled back up.
[what_to_bring] ice axes — sized to the climber's comfort.
[what_to_bring] crampons.
[approach] Gain the saddle by talus, drop steeply down the north side, ideally on snow, and then cross east to reach the couloir's foot.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
[descent_text] From the top-out, either bear right up the snowfield to the summit, or work down the gully to the south until the ledges to the west allow a scramble back up.
[descent_text] The exit is seldom corniced, though it can be steeper on the right.
[descent_text] Carry an axe, crampons and a helmet.

name: Main Squeeze
text: [overview] Pitches 2 and 3 (about M1-2, M2?) mostly wander over snow, with an occasional headwall, up to the dark chimney seen from the base.
